topics.chapterTitle: Defining Architecture Through Contracts and Failure Boundaries
topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: HarborDispatch begins as a request: “Let other applications submit work and check the result later.” A first design places a queue behind a network listener and starts several threads. That design may work for a demonstration, but it has not yet answered what happens when the response is lost, when the process stops, or when two clients choose the same request key. Architecture begins with those questions, before a diagram acquires boxes named after technologies.

blocks.text: This chapter turns the request into a contract that can be implemented and tested. The central distinction is between a property the application promises and a mechanism that might help implement it. A queue is a mechanism. “An acknowledged job survives the gateway process restarting” is a property. The latter determines whether an in-memory queue is sufficient.

topics.chapterTitle: Defining Architecture Through Contracts and Failure Boundaries
topics.title: 1.1.1 Separating Outcomes from Implementation Preferences
topics.summary: A requirement should describe something an observer can distinguish. “Use asynchronous processing” describes a preference about implementation. “A client receives a stable job key after durable acceptance and can retrieve the eventual result using that key” describes behavior. The second sentence leaves room for different thread models, databases, and transports while making the acceptance point meaningful.

blocks.text: For the teaching service, the input is an identifier and an integer from zero through one million. The result is the integer’s square. The identifier is an ASCII token of at most 64 bytes. These constraints make parsing, storage, and arithmetic bounded. They also make wrong-result detection independent of the worker: the test can compute an expected answer without trusting the remote implementation.

blocks.text: Separate functional outcomes from operational conditions. Functional outcomes include rejection of malformed input and stable replay of an accepted request. Operational conditions include maximum frame size, admitted backlog, request waiting time, and the behavior of shutdown. A successful arithmetic result does not compensate for an unbounded backlog. Conversely, bounded memory does not compensate for returning the wrong job’s result.

blocks.text: Avoid writing performance targets without a measurement boundary. “Fast” cannot be tested. An illustrative target such as “ninety-nine percent of status queries complete within 100 milliseconds under the named workload” identifies a population, a statistic, a threshold, and a workload. It is still incomplete until the team states whether time begins at the client, the load balancer, or the server’s handler. These are design questions, not decoration for a benchmark report.

topics.chapterTitle: Defining Architecture Through Contracts and Failure Boundaries
topics.title: 1.1.2 Defining Preconditions, Postconditions, and Invariants
topics.summary: A precondition describes what must hold before an operation is valid. A postcondition describes what the operation establishes when it succeeds. An invariant describes a property preserved across valid operations. For submit(key, input), the precondition includes a valid key and a bounded integer. A successful acceptance establishes that the gateway has a retrievable record. The invariant is that one key cannot silently acquire a different input later.

blocks.text: That invariant has consequences. A repeated key with the same canonical input is a replay; a repeated key with a different input is a conflict. Returning “already exists” without comparing the input loses the distinction. A client that accidentally reuses a key for another job could otherwise receive an unrelated result while believing its new request succeeded.

blocks.text: A C++ type can express part of the contract but not all of it. std::int64_t establishes a representation range, not the business limit of one million. A std::string can contain spaces, null bytes, and arbitrary lengths; it does not establish an identifier grammar. The boundary must validate these properties and create a domain value only after validation. topics.chapterTitle: Defining Architecture Through Contracts and Failure Boundaries
topics.title: 1.2.1 Assigning an Authoritative Owner to Each Fact
topics.summary: A fact needs an owner that can answer conflicting claims. The gateway owns whether a request has been accepted. The worker owns its receipt and computed result. The client owns whether it has observed an answer. Those facts can legitimately differ at the same moment. The worker may have committed a result while the gateway still records the job as pending because the acknowledgment was lost.

blocks.text: Draw the ownership graph separately from the call graph. In the call graph, the gateway contacts the worker. In the ownership graph, neither process may rewrite the other’s database directly. This prevents a shortcut in which the gateway “repairs” a remote result by editing a file it happens to reach. Such a shortcut bypasses the worker’s transaction, validation, and audit boundaries.

topics.title: 1.2.2 Separating Volatile, Durable, and Reconstructible State
topics.summary: Volatile state disappears when the process ends. Durable state is intended to survive the failures named by its storage contract. Reconstructible state can be rebuilt from another authoritative source. These categories answer different recovery questions and should not be collapsed into “stored somewhere.”

blocks.headingContext: 1.2.2 Separating Volatile, Durable, and Reconstructible State

blocks.text: The gateway’s socket read buffer is volatile. Losing it may require a client retry, which is acceptable because request identity is stable. A pending accepted job is not merely a socket buffer; it must remain available after a restart. The dispatcher therefore reads pending work from durable records instead of treating a transient queue as the only copy.

The dispatcher therefore reads pending work from durable records instead of treating a transient queue as the only copy.
blocks.headingContext: 1.2.2 Separating Volatile, Durable, and Reconstructible State

blocks.text: A cache of status responses is reconstructible if the database remains authoritative. Its loss is primarily a performance event. A cache used as the only copy of accepted jobs has become a database regardless of its product name. Its eviction, persistence, replication, and recovery settings must then satisfy the stronger role.

blocks.text: Durability is always conditional. A process restart, operating-system crash, host loss, storage-device failure, and regional outage are different fault scopes. A local database can preserve records across a process restart while failing completely with the disk. Naming the intended fault scope avoids claiming disaster recovery from evidence that only exercised a process restart.

topics.title: 1.3.1 Distinguishing Safety from Liveness
topics.summary: A safety property forbids a bad event. “A key is never associated with two different inputs” is a safety property. A liveness property requires progress. “Every accepted job eventually completes when dependencies recover and resources remain available” is a conditional liveness property. A system can preserve safety by refusing work forever, but that is not a useful service.

A liveness property requires progress. “Every accepted job eventually completes when dependencies recover and resources remain available” is a conditional liveness property. blocks.text: The distinction makes failure handling more precise. When the worker is unavailable, the gateway can preserve accepted intent and stop claiming completion. It may continue accepting jobs until the documented pending limit is reached. Once that limit is reached, rejecting additional new jobs preserves bounded resource use. The service loses some availability, but it does not invent success or erase accepted work.

The service loses some availability, but it does not invent success or erase accepted work.

blocks.text: A liveness claim needs assumptions. Eventual completion cannot be guaranteed if the worker remains absent forever, if the input is permanently invalid, or if the storage is irreparably lost. State the recovery assumptions rather than replacing them with the word “eventual.” Later chapters explore fairness and poison messages, which can prevent progress even when the network is functioning.

blocks.text: Tests should name the property under investigation. A duplicate-delivery test checks a safety boundary. A worker-restart test checks progress under a specific recovery schedule. Combining both in one scenario is useful, but neither result establishes all possible schedules.

topics.title: 1.3.2 Choosing the Smallest Architecture That Preserves the Contract
topics.summary: Begin with a design whose state transitions can be inspected. A modular application with one authoritative store may satisfy the workload more clearly than many independent services. Distribution becomes justified when a requirement needs independent deployment, failure containment, scaling, access control, or ownership. Each new remote boundary adds serialization, latency, ambiguity, and operational work.

reading.title: Practice and implementation lab
paragraphs: Add a maximum key length test and a test containing an embedded null byte. Then write a one-page contract for a different calculation, such as the sum of a bounded vector. State the element limit, numeric range, overflow policy, request identity rule, and meaning of acceptance. Do not choose a queue or database until those properties are written.

Solution reasoning. A null byte inside a key must be rejected by this grammar even though std::string can store it. A 65-byte key must fail before storage. For a vector sum, either establish a bound that proves the accumulator cannot overflow or implement checked addition with an explicit error outcome. Using a wider integer without deriving its limit does not complete the argument.
Chapter takeaway. Architecture becomes testable when success, ownership, identity, and uncertainty are specified as observable contracts.

nodes.label: Check the final state
code: // 101 is invalid; 8 is rejected as full.

overview.explanation: Solid arrows show conditional execution and the final check. Each submit call returns before the next call begins; this example has no concurrent producer.

focus.title: Check first, mutate second
focus.code:
std::vector<int> jobs{4};constexpr std::size_t capacity=2;
    auto submit=[&](int x){if(x<0||x>100||jobs.size()==capacity)return false;jobs.push_back(x);return true;};
explain: The queue starts with 4. constexpr makes capacity a compile-time constant equal to two.
[&] borrows jobs and capacity. || means logical OR; if any guard is true, return false ends the call. Only a passing call reaches push_back and returns true.
focus.what: Admission is a boundary: reject inputs outside 0–100 and requests that would exceed capacity.
focus.where: The lambda runs three times from the next source line.
focus.why: Keeping checks before mutation makes rejection easy to reason about and test.
focus.invariant: At this boundary, jobs.size() never exceeds two and a rejected call preserves its previous state.
focus.risk: Pushing first and checking later would briefly or permanently violate capacity. Concurrent callers would need synchronization; this code is a single-thread model.

focus.title: Test results and state together
explain: The calls run in order: 7 is accepted, 101 is invalid, and 8 finds the queue full.
The explicit comparison returns failure status 1 unless the vector is exactly {4,7}.
boolalpha prints true/false. The observed results are accepted=true, invalid=false, full=false, count=2.
focus.what: The test checks both returned decisions and the state those decisions leave behind.
focus.where: The fixture is inside main, after all three submissions.
focus.why: A boolean alone could hide an unwanted state change; checking the vector catches it.
focus.invariant: Only one additional job is stored. Invalid and full calls leave it unchanged.
focus.risk: Calling false an error category loses the distinction between invalid input and temporary saturation; Book VIII’s outcome type addresses that need.
